name: F-6 Marriage Migrant visa (spouse of a Korean national)

requirements.blocker_text: Requires a legally registered marriage to a Korean citizen, with evidence the relationship is genuine (not a sham marriage) -- immigration officers specifically screen marriage authenticity as one of the three core review areas alongside income and communication.

The Korean-citizen sponsor must meet an income threshold published annually by the Minister of Justice, scaled to household size -- family income (including the foreign spouse's own income, if any) can be combined to meet it.
requirements.fix_path: Document combined household income at or above the current year's published threshold for the applicable household size.

requirements.blocker_text: Requires evidence the couple can communicate -- TOPIK Level 1 or higher, or documented shared language history (e.g. the sponsor lived in the spouse's home country for a year or more, or the couple shared a common third language for a year or more).
requirements.fix_path: Complete a TOPIK Level 1 exam or document an alternative qualifying communication history.

requirements.blocker_text: The Korean sponsor is barred from sponsoring another foreign spouse if they have sponsored one within the preceding 5 years, and a naturalised Korean who acquired citizenship through marriage cannot sponsor a new foreign spouse until 3 years have passed since naturalisation.

evidence_required.document: Marriage certificate and civil registration documents
Income documentation meeting the current Ministry of Justice income notice
TOPIK certificate or equivalent communication-history evidence

outcome.duration_length: renewed indefinitely as long as the marriage is maintained

sources.title: Easy-to-Find Practical Law (easylaw.go.kr, Ministry of Government Legislation) -- Immigrants by marriage: International Marriage, Status and Nationality
Korvia -- How to apply F-6 Visa from Overseas Korean Consulate, corroborating the 5-year prior-sponsorship restriction and the 3-year post-naturalisation restriction

notes: F-6 is one of the most favourable family routes in this entire dataset: unlike Poland's spouse-of-citizen track (still a multi-year residence requirement before permanent residence) or most other countries' marriage routes, F-6 holders can reach a simplified permanent residence (F-5-2) or simplified naturalisation after just 2 years -- confirmed identically across easylaw.go.kr (the Ministry of Government Legislation's own official plain-language legal explainer, a genuine tier-1 source) and multiple independent secondary sources. Korea's Nationality Act offers marriage-based applicants an even faster alternate track for some cases: naturalisation after 3 years of marriage plus 1+ year of Korean residence, an alternative to the 2-years-continuous-residence-while-married standard track, useful for spouses who married abroad and moved to Korea partway through the marriage. dual_citizenship_allowed is true here specifically because F-6-to-citizenship naturalisation is one of Korea's narrow, explicitly-permitted dual-nationality exceptions (alongside the exceptional-talent naturalisation track) -- contrasted with kr_e7_designated_activities and kr_d8_corporate_investment, where dual_citizenship_allowed is false under Korea's general single-nationality rule; this is a genuine structural difference between naturalisation pathways within the same country, not an inconsistency. income requirement is modeled with an 'exists' test rather than a fixed KRW figure because the Ministry of Justice publishes the threshold annually and it varies by household size -- multiple secondary sources cite differing illustrative figures (e.g. KRW 25.19 million for a 2-person household as of one 2026 source), but no single fixed number applies universally, so a fixed hard-coded amount would misrepresent the actual rule; this mirrors how Saudi Arabia's family-sponsorship threshold was handled honestly rather than forcing a false precision.
